one_line_idea: A paired same-image comparison protocol for detectors, using per-image score differences with sign-flip permutation tests, shrinks comparison uncertainty enough to change published accept/reject conclusions at fixed test-set size.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detector comparisons report unpaired AP deltas on a shared test set, and small claimed gains (under 0.5 AP) are routinely accepted without any variance accounting.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because per-image difficulty is the dominant variance component and is shared between models evaluated on the same images, a paired design that tests the distribution of per-image metric differences removes that shared component and yields far tighter confidence intervals than image-level bootstrap of each model separately.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On COCO val2017, paired sign-flip confidence intervals for AP-proxy differences between five nearby public detector pairs will be at least 2x narrower than unpaired bootstrap intervals, and at least one of the five pairs will flip between significant and not-significant relative to the unpaired protocol; kill the idea if the average interval-width ratio is under 1.3x or if zero of five pairs change status.
why_important: This is a direct debunk-to-repair conversion: instead of another audit showing detection deltas are noise, it ships a drop-in comparison protocol that makes small-margin conclusions defensible without collecting new data.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Paired tests are standard in ML broadly, but a pre-registered paired-permutation protocol for COCO-style AP with a measured interval-shrinkage factor and conclusion-flip audit appears unpublished for detection.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Evaluate 10 public detectors on COCO val2017, compute per-image matched-detection quality scores, then compare paired sign-flip intervals against unpaired bootstrap intervals for all 45 pairs and count status flips among the 5 closest pairs.
main_risk: AP is a set-level statistic that does not decompose exactly into per-image contributions, so the paired proxy may rank models slightly differently than corpus-level AP and the repair could be rejected on fidelity grounds.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Practitioners treat the shared test set as already controlling for difficulty and assume reported AP deltas are comparable without explicit pairing.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If between-image variance is small relative to within-image matching noise, pairing buys little and interval widths will barely change.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inference of 10 MMDetection model-zoo checkpoints (e.g., Faster R-CNN, RetinaNet, DETR, YOLOX variants) on COCO val2017 plus permutation statistics runs in under 8 hours on one consumer GPU; all data and models public.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Seed-variance complaints exist for detection, but a packaged MDD certificate with hierarchical decomposition over image sampling and seeds, plus a retroactive reclassification audit, appears missing.

one_line_idea: Cryptographic canary items for vision benchmarks: seeding test sets with arbitrary-labeled canary images gives benchmark hosts a statistically powered detector of training-on-test contamination that works as a protocol, not a forensic investigation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmark hosts cannot verify whether submitted models trained on test data; current contamination arguments rely on circumstantial evidence assembled long after the fact.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Because canary labels are arbitrary (assigned by a keyed rule, not visual content), any above-chance canary accuracy is attributable to test-set exposure, so a small canary set embedded at benchmark creation yields a contamination test with quantifiable power and false-positive control, independent of model internals.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] With 200 canaries embedded in a benchmark, a model finetuned on a training set contaminated with the labeled test data will be detected at over 95% power at a 1% false-positive rate, while clean-trained models of any strength stay at chance on canaries; kill the idea if strong clean models exceed chance on canaries (visual-similarity leakage breaks arbitrariness) or if detection power at 200 canaries falls below 60%.
why_important: This is protocol-level infrastructure: it converts contamination disputes into a routine statistical check that benchmark hosts run at submission time, complementing mechanism-focused memorization research without overlapping it.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Canary strings are established for language-model privacy auditing; a benchmark-side canary protocol for vision test-set contamination with power analysis appears undeveloped.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct a benchmark from ImageNet-subset classes plus 200 keyed-label canaries, finetune ViT-B and ResNet-50 (timm) under clean and deliberately contaminated regimes at several contamination fractions, and trace detection power versus canary count.
main_risk: Sophisticated contamination (training on test images without labels, or on near-duplicates) would evade label-keyed canaries, limiting the protocol to the crudest contamination mode.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Contamination policing is assumed to require either data-pipeline transparency or post-hoc similarity forensics, both impractical at scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Public leaderboards may face mostly unlabeled-image contamination, for which this protocol is blind by design, making its deterrence value marginal.
fastest_falsification_experiment: A dozen short finetunes of timm ViT-B/ResNet-50 on ImageNet-100-scale subsets with injected canaries run in about 2 days total on one A100; all components public or scripted.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: keyed canary embedding vs no canaries under controlled contamination
family_fingerprint.measurement_family: detection power at fixed false-positive rate

one_line_idea: Noise-ceiling-normalized leaderboards: estimating each benchmark's inter-annotator ceiling and reporting scores as fractions of remaining headroom changes which improvements look meaningful, especially near saturation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Leaderboards report raw scores with no reference to the benchmark's annotation-noise ceiling, so a 0.5-point gain reads the same at 60% and at 95% of the achievable maximum.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Inter-annotator agreement data (double-annotated subsets that several public datasets already ship) supports estimating a per-benchmark, per-class noise ceiling, and headroom-normalized reporting reorders both class-level priorities and model-level conclusions in the saturation regime.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Using public double-annotation subsets to estimate ceilings on Cityscapes and LVIS, at least 20% of classes will show current best models within measurement noise of the ceiling (making further class gains unmeasurable), and headroom-normalized ranking will flip at least 1 of the top-3 model orderings on one benchmark; kill the idea if estimated ceilings exceed raw best scores by more than 10 points everywhere, meaning saturation is nowhere near and normalization changes nothing.
why_important: Prevents the community from spending compute on classes and benchmarks that are already measurement-limited and redirects it to real headroom, as a reporting capability rather than a critique.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Noise ceilings are standard in neuroscience model evaluation; systematic ceiling-normalized reporting for vision benchmarks appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Estimate per-class ceilings from annotator-pair agreement on the double-annotated subsets, propagate uncertainty, and re-render public leaderboard slices (top-10 checkpoints) in headroom units with flip analysis.
main_risk: Double-annotated subsets are small and possibly unrepresentative, giving ceiling estimates with error bars wide enough to swallow the conclusions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Raw metric points are treated as having constant meaning across the score range, and saturation talk stays qualitative.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Model errors and annotator disagreements may be qualitatively different, so agreement-based estimates may not bound achievable model scores in either direction.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Ceiling estimation from public agreement subsets plus re-scoring 10 public checkpoints (MMSegmentation for Cityscapes, MMDetection for LVIS) is inference-plus-analysis, about 1 day on one GPU; all public.

family_fingerprint.measurement_family: class saturation shares and top-rank flips

one_line_idea: Difficulty-matched test refresh: replacing stale test images with fresh ones matched on anchor-model difficulty profiles preserves model rankings while breaking URL-level and hash-level contamination, enabling routine benchmark rotation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Benchmarks cannot rotate their test sets without breaking comparability, because fresh images shift difficulty and invalidate historical numbers, so test sets stay static and contaminable for a decade.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] An image's difficulty profile (per-anchor-model scores across a frozen anchor ensemble) is a sufficient statistic for its effect on rankings, so sampling fresh images to match the joint difficulty-profile distribution of retired images yields a replacement set on which rankings and score levels are preserved for non-anchor models.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Swapping 50% of a COCO-classes evaluation set with difficulty-matched fresh images drawn from Open Images will preserve the ranking of 10 held-out public detectors with Kendall tau at least 0.9 and mean absolute score shift under 0.5 AP, versus tau under 0.8 for unmatched refresh; kill the idea if matched refresh does no better than unmatched or tau falls below 0.7.
why_important: Routine rotation is the strongest structural defense against test-set contamination and overfitting, and difficulty matching is the missing piece that keeps longitudinal comparability.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Difficulty estimation per item exists; using anchor-profile matching to certify ranking-preserving test refresh appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Score anchor and held-out detector pools on COCO val2017 and a relabeled Open Images candidate pool, run matched and random 50% swaps, and compare ranking preservation and score-level drift across 20 refresh replicates.
main_risk: Cross-dataset label-convention differences between the source and refresh pools could dominate the swap effect, confounding the difficulty-matching evaluation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Test sets are treated as irreplaceable artifacts whose rotation necessarily resets all historical comparisons.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Difficulty profiles from anchors may not span the factors that differentiate future models, so preservation for today's held-out pool may not extend to tomorrow's architectures.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Inference of ~16 public MMDetection checkpoints on COCO val2017 and an Open Images subset with shared classes takes about 1 day on one GPU; both datasets and all models public.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: difficulty-profile-matched vs random refresh sampling
family_fingerprint.measurement_family: ranking preservation and score drift under swaps

one_line_idea: Partial-pooling estimators for rare-class metrics: hierarchical shrinkage of per-class AP/IoU stabilizes long-tail leaderboards, halving bootstrap rank volatility and changing which long-tail methods win.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Rare-class metrics on long-tail benchmarks rest on a handful of instances per class, so per-class scores and the rare-split averages built from them are wildly unstable, yet leaderboards report them as point values.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Per-class scores share structure (class prototypes, frequency bands), so an empirical-Bayes partial-pooling estimator borrows strength across classes to produce rare-split estimates that are both lower-variance and better predictors of scores on a second sample, changing method comparisons that currently hinge on noise.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On LVIS v1 val, partial-pooled rare-class AP will reduce bootstrap rank volatility among 6 public long-tail methods by at least a factor of 2 and will flip at least 1 published pairwise ordering; cross-validated prediction of held-out-split class scores will improve (lower MSE) for at least 80% of rare classes; kill the idea if volatility reduction is under 1.2x or held-out prediction does not improve.
why_important: Long-tail research currently optimizes against noise on the rare split; a stabilized estimator redirects the subfield toward real effects and is adoptable by the benchmark host directly.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Empirical-Bayes shrinkage is classical; its application to long-tail vision leaderboards with a rank-stability and flip audit appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fit hierarchical models over per-class AP of 6 public LVIS checkpoints, compare raw vs pooled estimates under bootstrap resampling and split-half validation, and audit ordering flips on the rare split.
main_risk: Shrinkage pulls genuinely exceptional per-class performances toward the mean, and methods specializing on a few rare classes would be systematically under-credited.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Per-class point estimates are treated as the honest raw data, with shrinkage viewed as statistical tampering.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If method effects on rare classes are strongly class-idiosyncratic, no pooling structure fits and the estimator's cross-validation advantage disappears.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Scoring 6 public LVIS checkpoints (MMDetection configs and the public Detic release) plus hierarchical fitting runs in about 8 hours on one GPU; all public.
